comm.t: Medhas, the seer, resumes the story for King Suratha and the merchant Samādhi. Chapter 6 ended with Śumbha’s order to Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa (6.21–24): go with a large army and bring the Goddess back, dragged by the hair or bound — or kill her if there is any doubt in battle. In recitation this mantra carries the bīja ॐ, which belongs to the pāṭha, not to the verse.

mantras.lit: Then those Daityas, commanded, with Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa at their head, furnished with a fourfold army, with weapons raised, went.
mantras.tr: So commanded, the Daityas marched out, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa at their head, with an army of all four arms and their weapons raised.

comm.t: The order of 6.21–24 is carried out. The army is चतुरङ्ग, the four divisions of the classical Indian army; the verses that follow show each of them ending in Kālī’s mouth: elephants (7.10), then warriors, horses and chariots with their drivers (7.11).
Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa are the generals of Śumbha and Niśumbha. Their names (caṇḍa ‘fierce’, muṇḍa ‘shaven, a head’) will give the Goddess one of her best-known names at the end of this chapter (7.27).

mantras.lit: Then they saw the Goddess, gently smiling, seated upon the lion, on a great golden peak of the king of mountains.
mantras.tr: There they saw the Goddess, a faint smile on her face, seated on her lion upon a great golden summit of the king of mountains.

comm.t: The king of mountains is the Himālaya, where the gods praised her (5.7) and where Śumbha’s servants first saw her ‘lighting up the Himālaya’ (5.90). Her faint smile before an advancing army is the same composure she showed Śumbha’s messenger (5.104 onward).
A modern reading: the text sets a still, smiling figure against an armed host. Her calm is not ignorance of danger; the next verses show what it holds in reserve.

mantras.anvaya: ते तां दृष्ट्वा उद्यताः (सन्तः) तां समादातुम् उद्यमं चक्रुः; तथा अन्ये आकृष्टचापासिधराः तत्समीपगाः (अभवन्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: some made an attempt to seize her (उद्यमं चक्रुः); others, armed, came close (तत्समीपगाः, with a verb ‘were’ understood).
mantras.lit: Having seen her, they, eager, made an attempt to seize her; and likewise others, holding drawn bows and swords, (were) going near her.
mantras.tr: Seeing her, some made ready and moved to seize her; others, with bows drawn and swords bared, closed in around her.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Some’ is supplied to set ते against अन्ये (‘others’); the second clause has no finite verb, and ‘closed in’ renders the compound तत्समीपगाः.

comm.t: The asuras try to do what Śumbha ordered: take her alive (समादातुम्). Some move to seize her, the others surround her with weapons ready.
Her quiet in 7.3 and their bustle here stand side by side; the turn comes in the next verse, where the first thing that moves in her is anger.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: Ambikā grew angry; and with that anger her face turned black.
mantras.lit: Then Ambikā made great anger towards those enemies; and with the anger her face then became ink-coloured.
mantras.tr: Then Ambikā’s anger rose high against those enemies, and in her wrath her face turned black as ink.

comm.t: The anger is the cause (कोपेन) of the darkening: the dark face is the immediate prelude to Kālī’s emergence in the next verse. The Goddess is called Ambikā, the name used through chapters 5–6 for the form that came out of Pārvatī’s body (5.87).
Traditionally Kālī is understood as the Devī’s own wrath made visible: the text moves in one line from anger (कोप) to a dark face, and in the next from the brow to a separate figure.

mantras.anvaya_en: Source in the ablative (from her frowning forehead), subject with epithets (काली करालवदना असिपाशिनी), participle as verb.
mantras.lit: From the surface of her forehead, crooked with a frown, there swiftly came forth Kālī, of dreadful face, bearing sword and noose.
mantras.tr: From her forehead, knotted in a frown, there sprang at once Kālī, terrible of face, armed with sword and noose.

comm.t: Kālī is born from the Goddess’s frowning brow. This is a different event from 5.88, where Pārvatī herself turns dark and is called Kālikā after Ambikā has come out of her body; here Kālī comes out of Ambikā.

The Śākta tradition reads the sequence of 7.5–6 as anger taking form: the Devī’s wrath does not stay a mood but becomes a goddess who acts. Sword and noose are her first attributes; 7.7–8 complete the picture.
A modern reading: the fierce form does not come from outside the gracious one. The same Goddess who smiled in 7.3 frowns here, and what she sends out is still herself.

mantras.anvaya_en: No verb: four nominative epithets of Kālī, continuing 7.6.
mantras.lit: Bearing a strange khaṭvāṅga, ornamented with a garland of men, clothed in a leopard’s skin, exceedingly terrible with her dried flesh —
mantras.tr: She bore a strange skull-staff and wore a garland of human heads; a leopard’s hide was her garment, and her withered flesh made her more terrible still.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Skull-staff’ and ‘human heads’ give the traditional sense of खट्वाङ्ग and नरमाला; the verse has no verb, and ‘she bore … wore … was’ is supplied.

comm.t: The portrait of Kālī continues: weapon, ornament, garment, body. Every item belongs to the cremation ground and the ascetic who lives there.
Verses 7.6–8 are traditionally taken as the classic description of Kālī and Cāmuṇḍā, and they agree closely with the hymn’s address to Cāmuṇḍā in chapter 11 (11.21: दंष्ट्राकरालवदने शिरोमालाविभूषणे).

samasa.literal: she by whom the faces of the quarters are filled with a roar

morph.note: A bahuvrīhi whose relative pronoun is instrumental (यया ‘by whom’): the participle आपूरित (आ + √पॄ, causative ‘filled’) keeps its passive sense inside the compound.

mantras.anvaya: (सा काली) अतिविस्तारवदना जिह्वाललनभीषणा निमग्नारक्तनयना नादापूरितदिङ्मुखा (आसीत्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: No verb: four more nominative epithets of Kālī, closing the description begun in 7.6.
mantras.lit: Having a very wide mouth, terrifying with the lolling of her tongue, having sunken red eyes, having the quarters filled with her roar —
mantras.tr: Her mouth gaped wide, her lolling tongue struck terror, her sunken eyes were red, and her roar filled every quarter of the sky.
mantras.tr_note: The epithets are turned into short clauses; nothing is added.

comm.t: The description ends with the mouth, the tongue, the eyes and the voice. The wide mouth is not ornament: it is how she will fight (7.9–13), swallowing the army whole.
The roar that fills the quarters answers the battle-cry of the Daityas. In chapter 8 Caṇḍikā will ask Kālī to open this same mouth wide (8.53: विस्तीर्णं वदनं कुरु) to drink the blood of Raktabīja.

mantras.anvaya_en: Subject सा with two participles (अभिपतिता, घातयन्ती); the main verb अभक्षयत with its object तत् बलम्; the locative सैन्ये … सुरारीणाम् gives where.
mantras.lit: She, having rushed with speed, slaying the great asuras, there in the army of the gods’ enemies devoured that force.
mantras.tr: She fell upon them with a rush, cutting down the great asuras, and there in the ranks of the gods’ enemies she devoured that host.

comm.t: Kālī’s first act is to charge into the army and eat it. The next four verses spell out how: elephants, horses, chariots and warriors go into her mouth.
Kālī devours what she fights; nothing of the enemy is left over. The tradition reads her mouth as the place where every form ends, which is why the same image returns with Raktabīja in chapter 8.

Verbs of throwing put the place into which something is thrown in the locative: मुखे चिक्षेप ‘threw into the mouth’.

mantras.anvaya: (सा) पार्ष्णिग्राहाङ्कुशग्राहियोधघण्टासमन्वितान् वारणान् एकहस्तेन समादाय मुखे चिक्षेप।
mantras.anvaya_en: Absolutive (समादाय) then main verb (चिक्षेप), sharing the object वारणान् with its long qualifying compound.
mantras.lit: Seizing with one hand the elephants together with rear-riders, goad-holders, warriors and bells, she threw them into her mouth.
mantras.tr: Gathering up the war elephants in one hand, with their rear-riders, their drivers, their fighting men and their bells, she flung them into her mouth.

comm.t: The elephants, the first of the four arms of the army (7.2), go first — crew, harness and all, scooped up in a single hand.
A modern reading: the list is deliberately exhaustive. Nothing the asura army brings — its riders, its drivers, even its bells — is too large or too small to be taken in.

mantras.anvaya: तथा एव योधं तुरगैः (सह), रथं सारथिना सह वक्त्रे निक्षिप्य दशनैः अतिभैरवं चर्वयन्ती (आसीत्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two objects with their companions (योधं तुरगैः, रथं सारथिना सह), the absolutive निक्षिप्य, and the participle चर्वयन्ती as predicate.
mantras.lit: Just so, having thrust into her mouth the warrior with the horses, the chariot with the charioteer, she was chewing them most horribly with her teeth.
mantras.tr: In the same way she thrust into her mouth the horsemen with their horses and the chariots with their drivers, and crunched them hideously between her teeth.
mantras.tr_note: The singulars योधम् and रथम् are collective, and are rendered as plurals; ‘horsemen’ renders योधं तुरगैः.

comm.t: After the elephants (7.10), the cavalry and the chariots: with the infantry in 7.12, the four arms of the army named in 7.2 are accounted for.
A modern reading: the narrative does not look away. The horror is meant to be felt, so that the power that protects the world is not mistaken for something tame.

mantras.anvaya: (सा) एकं केशेषु जग्राह, अथ च अपरं ग्रीवायाम् (जग्राह); अन्यं च एव पादेन आक्रम्य (अपोथयत्), अन्यम् उरसा अपोथयत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Four victims: two seized (by the hair, by the neck) with जग्राह, two crushed with अपोथयत् (one after being trampled, one with her chest).
mantras.lit: One she seized by the hair, and then another by the neck; and likewise, having trampled another with her foot, (she crushed him); another she crushed with her chest.
mantras.tr: One she caught by the hair, another by the throat; one she trampled underfoot, and another she crushed against her breast.
mantras.tr_note: The second ‘crushed’ is shared by the two halves of the second line; the readable version lets ‘trampled’ stand for both.

comm.t: The foot soldiers, the fourth arm of the army: each is dealt with differently — by the hair, by the neck, by the foot, by the chest. The rhythm एकम् … अपरम् … अन्यम् … अन्यम् gives the speed of the slaughter.

mantras.anvaya: तैः असुरैः मुक्तानि शस्त्राणि तथा महास्त्राणि च (सा) रुषा मुखेन जग्राह; (तानि) दशनैः मथितानि अपि (अकरोत्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Main clause: she caught the weapons in her mouth; a second, verbless clause adds that her teeth crushed them as well.
mantras.lit: And the weapons and likewise the great missiles hurled by those asuras she caught with her mouth in fury, and (they were) crushed by her teeth as well.
mantras.tr: The weapons and the great missiles the asuras hurled at her she caught in her mouth in her fury, and ground them to pieces between her teeth.

comm.t: Even the army’s weapons are eaten. Hand weapons (शस्त्र) and missiles (अस्त्र) are named separately, so that nothing the asuras can use against her is left out.
In the battles of chapters 2–3 the Goddess cut the asuras’ weapons down with her own, ‘as if in play’ (2.50, 3.4); here Kālī simply swallows them. The fierce form does not parry: she takes in.

mantras.anvaya_en: Three verbs, three objects: the whole army trampled (ममर्द), some devoured (अभक्षयत्), others struck down (अताडयत्).
mantras.lit: That whole army of the mighty, evil-minded asuras she crushed; and some she devoured, and others likewise she struck.
mantras.tr: She trampled that whole army of mighty, evil-minded asuras: some she devoured, and others she beat to the ground.

comm.t: A summary verse: the army of 7.2 is destroyed by trampling, eating and striking. The epithets बलिनाम् and दुरात्मनाम् are set against each other: strength in the service of a wicked mind.

flags.uncertain: The first च may also link the two verbs (‘she crushed and devoured’, with अन्यान् the object of the next clause); the sense is unchanged.

mantras.anvaya_en: One verb (जग्मुः) for all; the three participial groups say how each set of asuras died.
mantras.lit: Some struck down by the sword, some beaten by the khaṭvāṅga, and likewise (others) struck by the tips of her teeth — the asuras went to destruction.
mantras.tr: Some fell to her sword, some to her skull-staff, and others to the points of her teeth: so the asuras perished.

comm.t: The three weapons of the slaughter are the three attributes of 7.6–8: the sword (असि), the khaṭvāṅga, and the mouth with its teeth. Her iconography is not decoration; each item is used.

mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is the object of दृष्ट्वा (‘seeing the army felled’); the main clause is चण्डः … कालीम् अभिदुद्राव.
mantras.lit: Having seen that whole army of the asuras laid low in a moment, Caṇḍa rushed at that exceedingly terrifying Kālī.
mantras.tr: When Caṇḍa saw the whole asura army laid low in a moment, he rushed at Kālī, terrible as she was.

comm.t: The army is gone, and the first general attacks. The opening half-line repeats 6.19 (क्षणेन तद्बलं सर्वम्), where the lion destroyed Dhūmralocana’s army in a moment: the text marks each rout with the same words.

mantras.anvaya: महासुरः (चण्डः) महाभीमैः शरवर्षैः, मुण्डः च सहस्रशः क्षिप्तैः चक्रैः तां भीमाक्षीं छादयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two subjects with their instruments — Caṇḍa with arrows, Muṇḍa with discuses — share the one verb छादयामास.
mantras.lit: The great asura covered that terrible-eyed one with most dreadful showers of arrows, and Muṇḍa with discuses hurled by the thousand.
mantras.tr: The great asura Caṇḍa buried the dread-eyed goddess under volleys of fearsome arrows, and Muṇḍa under discuses hurled by the thousand.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Caṇḍa’ is supplied: महासुरः continues the subject of 7.16.

comm.t: Both generals now attack together: Caṇḍa with arrows, Muṇḍa with discuses. ‘Covered’ (छादयामास) is the image of a storm of weapons that hides the target from sight.

flags.uncertain: महासुरः could also be read in apposition to मुण्डः (‘the great asura Muṇḍa covered her with arrows and discuses’). Since 7.16 makes Caṇḍa the attacker, he is taken as the subject of the first line.

mantras.anvaya_en: A simile: the discuses entering her mouth shone as very many suns (would) entering the belly of a cloud.
mantras.lit: Those many discuses, entering her mouth, shone like very many orbs of the sun (entering) the belly of a cloud.
mantras.tr: The countless discuses vanishing into her mouth shone like a multitude of suns sinking into the heart of a dark cloud.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Vanishing’ and ‘sinking’ render the participle ‘entering’, which the simile shares.

comm.t: Muṇḍa’s discuses do not wound her: they go into her mouth, as the weapons did in 7.13. The simile matches colour with colour — the bright discs are suns, the black mouth of Kālī (7.5) is a rain-cloud.

samasa.type: tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, a karmadhāraya (करालं वक्त्रम्, दुर्दर्शाः दशनाः) and the adverb अन्तर्

samasa.sense: her gaping mouth shining with fearsome teeth
samasa.alt: Because काली and कराल meet without any sandhi, काली can also be taken as a separate nominative, the subject of the verse (‘Kālī, blazing with fearsome teeth within her dreadful mouth’). The Gita Press prints the whole as one compound, and it is kept so here; the meaning does not change.

morph.note: Perfect of √हस्: the reduplicated h becomes j (ज-हास), with vṛddhi in the third singular.
Neuter accusative used as an adverb, like द्रुतम् (7.6) and अतिभैरवम् (7.11).

mantras.anvaya: ततः कालीकरालवक्त्रान्तर्दुर्दर्शदशनोज्ज्वला भैरवनादिनी (सा) अतिरुषा भीमं जहास।
mantras.anvaya_en: Verb जहास with the adverbs अतिरुषा and भीमम्; the subject is given by two epithets.
mantras.lit: Then she who roars dreadfully, bright with the teeth hard to look at within Kālī’s dreadful mouth, laughed terribly in extreme fury.
mantras.tr: Then Kālī, roaring dreadfully, laughed a terrible laugh in her fury, the fearsome teeth in her gaping mouth flashing with light.
mantras.tr_note: The readable version makes Kālī the subject, as the alternative analysis of the compound allows; ‘flashing with light’ renders उज्ज्वला.

comm.t: Kālī laughs at the weapons that are meant to destroy her. Laughter and roar go together, and the mouth that swallowed the discuses now shines with its teeth.

Laughter in battle is a sign of the Goddess throughout the text: she laughs aloud in 2.32 (साट्टहासम्) and laughs as she drinks in 3.34 (जहास), and Śivadūtī’s laughter terrifies the asuras in 8.38 and 9.23. It is the fury of a power that cannot be harmed; the अट्टहास returns in 7.23.

Imperfect of the rudhādi root √छिद्, which inserts the nasal infix in its strong stem (छिनद्-/छिनत्). After the augment a the ch is doubled to cch (छे च, 6.1.73).
√धाव् is ubhayapada; here the ātmanepada imperfect (-त), while 7.21 has the parasmaipada अभ्यधावत्.

mantras.anvaya: देवी च महासिंहम् उत्थाय चण्डम् अधावत; अस्य केशेषु च गृहीत्वा तेन असिना शिरः अच्छिनत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: mounting the lion (absolutive उत्थाय with its object), she rushed at Caṇḍa (अधावत); and, seizing him by the hair, she cut off his head with that sword.
mantras.lit: And having risen onto the great lion, the Goddess rushed at Caṇḍa; and having seized him by the hair, she cut off his head with that sword.
mantras.tr: Mounting the great lion, the Goddess charged at Caṇḍa, seized him by the hair, and with that sword struck off his head.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Mounting’ renders उत्थाय with the accusative: literally ‘rising up onto’.

comm.t: Caṇḍa is killed exactly as Śumbha had ordered the Goddess to be treated: seized by the hair (केशेष्वाकृष्य, 6.23). देवी here is Kālī, the subject since 7.16; she charges on the lion that carried the Goddess in 7.3, and ‘that sword’ is the one she was born holding (असिपाशिनी, 7.6). Note on the text: the Gita Press digital file printed महासिं हं, with a space inside the word, which could be misread as ‘great sword’ plus a cry ‘haṃ’. Both witnesses (GRETIL, Freund) read महासिंहं as one word, and the text has been corrected accordingly (corrections.json, 7.20).

mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: Muṇḍa’s charge (with the absolutive दृष्ट्वा), and Kālī’s answer (अपातयत्).
mantras.lit: Then Muṇḍa, having seen Caṇḍa struck down, rushed at her; she, in fury, felled him too to the ground, struck with the sword.
mantras.tr: Seeing Caṇḍa fallen, Muṇḍa charged at her; and she in her fury struck him with her sword and brought him to the ground as well.

comm.t: The second general meets the same end, in half a verse. The verb pair निपातितम् / अपातयत् ties the two deaths together: as Caṇḍa was felled, so Muṇḍa is felled.

mantras.lit: Then the army remaining from the slain, having seen Caṇḍa struck down and Muṇḍa of very great valour, fled, stricken with fear, to the quarters.
mantras.tr: Then the remnant of the army, seeing Caṇḍa slain and the mighty Muṇḍa too, scattered in terror to every quarter.

comm.t: The rout is complete. The first line repeats the half-line दृष्ट्वा चण्डं निपातितम् from 7.21, and adds Muṇḍa: what made Muṇḍa attack now makes the army run.

mantras.anvaya: काली च चण्डस्य शिरः मुण्डम् एव च गृहीत्वा चण्डिकाम् अभ्येत्य प्रचण्डाट्टहासमिश्रं प्राह।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject काली; two absolutives in sequence (गृहीत्वा, अभ्येत्य); main verb प्राह with an adverbial compound.
mantras.lit: And Kālī, having taken the head of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa too, approached Caṇḍikā and spoke, mingled with fierce loud laughter:
mantras.tr: Then Kālī took up the heads of Caṇḍa and of Muṇḍa, came to Caṇḍikā, and spoke, breaking into savage peals of laughter:
mantras.tr_note: ‘The heads … of Muṇḍa’ makes explicit what मुण्डम् means here.

comm.t: Kālī returns to the Goddess from whom she came and brings her the heads. The verse plays on one word: चण्डस्य, प्रचण्ड-, चण्डिकाम् — Caṇḍa’s head, Kālī’s ‘fiercer’ laughter, and Caṇḍikā, ‘the Fierce One’, to whom it is brought.
The Goddess is called Caṇḍikā at this point: the name the next verses will set beside the new name she gives to Kālī.

mantras.anvaya: मया अत्र चण्डमुण्डौ महापशू तव उपहृतौ। युद्धयज्ञे शुम्भं निशुम्भं च (त्वं) स्वयं हनिष्यसि।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: a passive statement with agent मया (‘are offered by me’), and a future with the understood subject त्वम्.
mantras.lit: By me, here, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, two great beasts, have been brought to you as an offering; in the sacrifice of battle you yourself will slay Śumbha and Niśumbha.
mantras.tr: Here I have brought you Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, two great victims for your offering. In this sacrifice of battle you yourself shall slay Śumbha and Niśumbha.

comm.t: Kālī presents the two heads as sacrificial victims (पशु) and calls the battle a sacrifice (युद्धयज्ञ). She leaves the last two victims, Śumbha and Niśumbha, to the Goddess herself — which is how the story will end (Niśumbha in 9.34–36, Śumbha in 10.27).

In the Śākta reading the war is a yajña with the Devī as its deity: the asuras are the victims, and what is offered is the power of ignorance and pride they stand for. This is an interpretation; the verse itself speaks only of the battle as a sacrifice.
A modern reading: the fierce power does its work and then lays the result at the feet of the gracious one. Kālī does not keep the victory for herself.

mantras.anvaya: ततः आनीतौ तौ चण्डमुण्डौ महासुरौ दृष्ट्वा कल्याणी चण्डिका कालीं ललितं वचः उवाच।
mantras.anvaya_en: Absolutive clause (दृष्ट्वा with the dual object), then the main clause: subject चण्डिका, verb उवाच, two objects कालीम् and वचः.
mantras.lit: Then, having seen those two great asuras Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa brought, the auspicious Caṇḍikā spoke gentle words to Kālī:
mantras.tr: Seeing the two great asuras, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, brought before her, gracious Caṇḍikā spoke gently to Kālī:

comm.t: After Kālī’s savage laughter (7.23), Caṇḍikā answers with gentle, charming words (ललितं वचः), and she is called कल्याणी, ‘the auspicious’. The text sets the two moods of the one Goddess side by side.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has both names: कल्याणी (name 324) and चण्डिका (name 755). The coincidence with ललितम् here is of vocabulary only; the two texts are separate works.

morph.note: Not a regular compound but a name explained by the verse itself (a nirvacana): she who seized Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa. The first syllable cā- recalls Caṇḍa (च-) and the rest is Muṇḍa (-मुण्डा).
Ablative of the relative pronoun, ‘from which (cause)’, answered by ततः ‘therefore’: यस्मात् … ततः ‘because … therefore’.
Past participle of a verb of motion, active in sense and feminine to agree with त्वम् (Kālī): ‘you have come’.
Simple future of √भू: भव्-इ-ष्य-सि. With ख्याता it means ‘you will be known’.

mantras.anvaya: देवि, यस्मात् त्वं चण्डं च मुण्डं च गृहीत्वा उपागता, ततः लोके चामुण्डा इति ख्याता भविष्यसि।
mantras.anvaya_en: A causal clause (यस्मात् … उपागता) and its correlative main clause (ततः … भविष्यसि), with the vocative देवि.
mantras.lit: Because you have come, having seized Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, therefore, O Goddess, you will be known in the world as ‘Cāmuṇḍā’.
mantras.tr: Since you have come to me bearing Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, you shall be known in the world, O Goddess, as Cāmuṇḍā.

comm.t: Caṇḍikā names Kālī: Cāmuṇḍā, the one who took Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa. The name is used from now on: in chapter 8 Caṇḍikā addresses Kālī as Cāmuṇḍā (8.53) and Cāmuṇḍā drinks Raktabīja’s blood (8.59–61); the hymn of chapter 11 salutes चामुण्डे मुण्डमथने (11.21).

In the liturgical tradition of the Saptaśatī the Navārṇa mantra, recited with the text, is addressed to this name (ऐं ह्रीं क्लीं चामुण्डायै विच्चे). In recitation this mantra closes with the bīja ॐ, which belongs to the pāṭha, not to the verse.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) remembers the same deed in name 756, चण्डमुण्डासुरनिषूदिनी, ‘slayer of the asuras Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa’, right after चण्डिका (755) — a specific echo of this chapter in a separate text.
A modern reading: the Goddess receives a new name for a deed, not by birth. The fierce power is honoured, named and given a place in the world.
